items.summary: For the first time since Independence, India’s Census will record the caste of all respondents, making Census 2027 one of the most significant demographic exercises in the country’s history. The new questionnaire expands from 29 categories in Census 2011 to 40 questions and includes information on caste, digital literacy, Aadhaar, mobile numbers, bank accounts, voter IDs, passports and more. But why is the caste question creating political debate? How will the open-column system work? And what lessons has the government drawn from the 2011 Socio-Economic and Caste Census? items.title: Hafta letters: NL investigations, cognitive biases, and independent media
items.summary: Deepak Team NL, I just wanted to thank you for the incredible work you are doing. Your recent investigations, especially on Yogi's ad campaign and the stone-laden truck at Jantar Mantar, are gaining a lot of attention. I am even seeing them being shared as cartoons referencing NL’s findings, even in the local language, Kannada. Whenever my friends forward them to me, I just smile and say I already knew about it because I subscribe to Newslaundry . Keep up the excellent work! Adil Adil here, environmental and safety engineer, raised near the Jhelum in Srinagar, living in Germany since 2016 and now working for Autobahn GmbH near Krefeld/Düsseldorf. Hence JhelumToRhine. Recent Haftas, from Khalra and state power to Meta, food taboos and religious processions, leave me with one question: would we defend the same principle if it protected someone we disagreed with? Governments seek votes; corporations seek profit. Neither is automatically our saviour. Culture deserves respect, but reverence alone shouldn’t restrict another person’s choices. Whether Carnival, Kanwar or Muharram fills our streets, rules should apply consistently. Lovely hearing Jayashree again; Mehraj brings a biased Kashmiri smile, and Rinchen is a refreshing addition. Perhaps democracy needs science’s finest habit: question even your own hypothesis, and change your mind when better evidence arrives. Adil | JhelumToRhine Shoor Veer In the last Hafta, a subscriber asked about resources for building an intellectual foundation to assess news and form opinions. For me, learning about cognitive biases has been enormously helpful in forming opinions rooted in evidence and detecting algorithmic manipulation. It's the single most important tool to have and to use against the tsunami of information we all deal with. In another discussion, Mehraj blamed liberalism for wokism. I find that argument completely bonkers. Woke culture is a direct result of social media, not any ideology. Liberalism puts the individual first, and wokism is all about collective guilt. Liberalism has stood against the witch hunts and mob justice that both right and left authoritarians have wrought. items.title: Introducing India’s first Court Downtime Tracker
items.summary: Is it just me? She wonders, staring at her screen. The court website has failed her yet again. She frantically refreshes, reboots, switches browsers - nothing works. A colleague in the corner says, "It's working fine for me." The mystery never stops. This isn't a one-off. It's just one example of the countless times each week that a court website fails to load for the average litigator, litigant, journalist, or legal researcher. Things get worse as you move down the judicial hierarchy. Court websites - a basic tool that facilitates access to justice in the digital age - are riddled with poor functionality, clunky interfaces, missing orders, mangled judge names, algebraic captchas and more. items.title: What the missing Arbitration Council reveals
items.summary: Chief Justice of India Surya Kant recently described the continued non-constitution of the Arbitration Council of India (ACI) as part of India's "credibility deficit" in becoming a preferred arbitral seat. 6 years after parliament enacted the statutory framework for the Council through the Arbitration and Conciliation (Amendment) Act, 2019, that criticism is difficult to dismiss. Parliament intended the ACI to serve as the institutional anchor of India's transition towards institutional arbitration and its ambition to become a preferred global arbitral seat. Despite that legislative ambition, the Council remains unconstituted. The issue has recently returned to the forefront of India's arbitration discourse following a pending Supreme Court petition in Anil Kalyandas Thanvi v. Union of India , in which the Court has issued notice on a plea alleging a continued regulatory vacuum in trade-association arbitrations, a vacuum the ACI was designed to remedy. Most commentary has understandably focused on why the ACI has not yet been constituted. The more important question is no longer why the Council remains unconstituted, but what the 6-year delay reveals about the institutional design parliament enacted in 2019. The problem parliament thought it was solving The ACI did not emerge in a vacuum. It was parliament's response to a diagnosis of India's arbitration landscape made by the High-Level Committee chaired by Justice BN Srikrishna in 2017. The Committee identified India's arbitration infrastructure as the principal obstacle to the growth of institutional arbitration. Institutional arbitration remained underdeveloped, quality standards varied across institutions and courts continued to perform functions that many mature arbitration jurisdictions had already entrusted to arbitral institutions. The ACI was conceived to strengthen confidence in institutional arbitration by providing a central coordinating body. items.summary: Facial recognition systems are increasingly used in public spaces in India, despite the absence of a comprehensive statutory framework governing their use. Imagine the concourse at Howrah station in Kolkata during rush hour with approximately a million commuters each day, along with a hundred cameras quietly scanning every face against a watchlist that only a few officials have ever seen in full. Walk through the corridors at the Ram Mandir in Ayodhya and similar machines are identifying faces using police records as worshippers wait for darshan. Ahmedabad’s “safe city” control room does the same for the whole city. The majority of these systems do not announce their presence, let alone ask for consent. Recent investigative reporting has revealed that much of the technology behind this surveillance comes from a Spanish company called Herta Security . Their facial recognition software reportedly runs on several thousand cameras across the country , which includes setups that would be illegal within the European Union, according to European legal scholars . items.title: Police need not obtain court permission before freezing bank accounts: Karnataka High Court
items.summary: The Karnataka High Court recently observed that the police cannot be first asked to approach the magistrate for permission to freeze a property, particularly proceeds of crime moving electronically from one bank account to other [State of Karnataka v Jar Gold Retail Pvt Ltd]. If police is asked to first approach a magistrate to debit freeze an account, the money may travel through ten accounts or simply vanish beyond retrieval by the time the procedural journey reaches its destination. Justice M Nagaprasanna made the observation while stressing on the importance of Section 106 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS) that allows police to seize a property on suspicion of crime. "The law cannot insist that the Police first complete a judicial pilgrimage while the proceeds of crime are electronically galloping from account to account. The distinction between the immediate preservative power under Section 106 of the BNSS and the adjudicatory mechanism under Section 107 of the BNSS becomes particularly vivid in this context," the Court said. The Court added that the seizure done under Section 106 is a preservatory measure intended to secure suspected tainted assets without need for judicial order. "Such seizure is a preservatory measure intended to secure suspected tainted assets during the investigation and ordinarily warrants no judicial interference during the pendency of investigation." Pertinently, the Court said that a debit freeze of a bank account is not required to travel through the procedural rigmarole contemplated under Section 107 of the BNSS. Imposing such a mandate would have disastrous consequences in today's time when the world is grappling with cybercrime "In such crimes, money does not merely move; it flies—from one account to another, through a labyrinth of mule accounts, often in a matter of seconds," the judge observed. Hence, a debit freeze must done as fast as possible for it to be effective, the Court said. "A naïve and gullible citizen may see his life’s savings disappear at the click of a mouse or the stroke of a key," the Court further said. "Therefore, the issue requires a broader and amicable resolution rather than being confined to the particular film," he stated. items.title: Kerala agrees to PMAY logo, beneficiaries may have to pay up to Rs 1 lakh
items.summary: The Kerala government has decided to proceed with the second phase of the Pradhan Mantri Awas Yojana-Urban (PMAY-U 2.0), agreeing to conditions that the previous Left Democratic Front (LDF) government had repeatedly opposed. This includes the display of the scheme’s logo on houses built for beneficiaries. The latest Cabinet decision also brings a financial burden for beneficiaries. Under the revised PMAY-U 2.0 guidelines, beneficiaries are required to bear 25% of the total project cost. The total assistance for each homeless beneficiary will remain at Rs 4 lakh. Of this, the Union government will contribute Rs 1.5 lakh and the Kerala government Rs 1 lakh. The remaining Rs 1.5 lakh will have to be shared between the municipality and the beneficiary, potentially taking the beneficiary’s contribution up to Rs 1 lakh. The decision was taken by the Cabinet on August 13, with the government opting to sign a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) with the Union government to implement PMAY-U 2.0. The state government has said the MoU is necessary to access around Rs 450 crore in Union government assistance. An estimated 30,000 beneficiaries are expected to receive houses under the scheme. Chief Minister VD Satheesan said the state would accept the logo requirement as part of the agreement, while making it clear that the Prime Minister’s photograph would not be displayed. “That is their (union government’s) condition that a logo should be placed outside the house. We won't keep the PM's photo but the logo we should keep,” Satheesan said after the Cabinet meeting. The LDF government had consistently rejected the requirement to display Union government branding on beneficiaries’ homes. As of February 2026, around 5,00,364 houses had been completed under the LIFE Mission out of 6,04,046 sanctioned houses, according to official figures. The issue had been framed by the LDF as one concerning the dignity and ownership of beneficiaries, rather than merely a branding requirement attached to a housing scheme. In 2023, then Chief Minister and current Leader of the Opposition Pinarayi Vijayan had rejected the proposal, arguing that housing was a basic human right and should not be turned into an advertisement for the Union government or the Prime Minister. “These are people’s own houses, and their dignity should not be questioned by placing logos on them,” Pinarayi had said. The issue resurfaced after Local Self Government Minister KM Shaji recently said the state was not opposed

items.title: ‘Will defeat forces and conspiracies against state govt': TN CM Vijay in first I-Day speech
items.summary: Follow TNM’s WhatsApp channel for news updates and story links. Marking his first Independence Day speech as Tamil Nadu Chief Minister, C Joseph Vijay said his government would “defeat the forces and conspiracies” working against it. “We all have cast our votes. You have elected your brother, your son, and made me the Chief Minister. From now on, all of you must continue to stand with our government. Only then we will be able to take good schemes and initiatives to the people,” Vijay said. “I, and everyone here, are servants of the people. We will defeat the forces and conspiracies working against our government,” he added. “Administratively, we are cooperating with the Union government, but ideologically, we continue to oppose its policies,” he said. He also reiterated his government’s commitment to protecting Tamil Nadu’s interests and state rights, saying anything that affected the state's interests or rights would be opposed. “It is our duty to protect Tamil Nadu from bribery and corruption. That is what our government is working towards,” he said. Vijay said his government was working towards establishing an honest and transparent administration and that there should be no compromise in public life. He said his government would continue schemes introduced by previous governments, including Amma Unavagam, introduced by former Chief Minister J Jayalalithaa, and the Breakfast scheme for school students, introduced by former CM MK Stalin. Vijay also announced that a gold ring gift scheme for newborns would be launched on September 15, marking the birth anniversary of former CM CN Annadurai. The assistance for disabled ex-servicemen has been increased from Rs 5,000 to Rs 7,000, while the monthly assistance for freedom fighters has been increased to Rs 23,000, he said.

items.summary: Follow TNM's WhatsApp channel for news updates and story links. The Telangana government has decided to release fee reimbursement funds in advance from the current academic year to ensure that students do not face difficulties in obtaining their certificates because of delays in payment. Telangana Chief Minister Revanth Reddy said Rs 2400 crore has been allocated for the programme, including Rs 250 crore towards advance payments. The government will provide around Rs 2300 crore every year for fee reimbursement, he said, urging eligible students to apply online so that the money can be directly credited to their accounts. Speaking at a programme held on Friday, August 14, to unveil the statues of social reformers Mahatma Jyothirao Phule and Savitri Phule, CM Revanth said his government was pursuing a series of reforms aimed at transforming the education system. As part of its skill-development efforts, the government is upgrading Industrial Training Institutes (ITIs) into Advanced Technology Centres (ATCs) in partnership with the Tata Group. Students enrolled in these centres will receive a monthly stipend of Rs 2000 while undergoing technical and skill-based training designed to improve their employability. The Chief Minister also criticised the previous BRS government, alleging that it did not adequately encourage education among weaker and marginalised sections. He said the present government was working to expand educational and employment opportunities for backward classes and other disadvantaged communities. CM Revanth also highlighted the Congress government's initiatives on Scheduled Caste categorisation and the caste census. items.title: Amid RSS march row, Karnataka Cabinet clears Bill regulating public spaces
items.summary: The Karnataka Cabinet on August 13 approved a bill to regulate the use of government premises and public property for private events, replacing a government order issued in 2025. The Karnataka Regulation of Use of Government Premises and Public Property Bill, 2026, seeks to govern the use of public spaces by private individuals, organisations, associations and societies. The existing government order requires organisations seeking to hold programmes or processions on public property to obtain prior permission from the police and revenue authorities at least three days before the event. The order had triggered political controversy after permission was denied to the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh (RSS) to hold a route march in Chittapur in October 2025. Chittapur is represented by Karnataka Home Minister Priyank Kharge, who has been a vocal critic of the RSS. The government order was issued shortly after Kharge wrote to then Chief Minister Siddaramaiah seeking restrictions on RSS activities in Karnataka. Kharge also proposed the new Bill in the August 13 Cabinet meeting. The 2025 order defined government property broadly to include land, buildings, structures, roads, parks, playgrounds, waterbodies and other immovable property owned or managed by government departments, local authorities, boards and corporations. Under the order, organisers were required to provide details of their organisation, the expected number of participants and other information sought by authorities. In the Chittapur case, the tahsildar had cited the RSS’s failure to provide details about the number of participants, registration documents and the use of lathis and other weapons while denying permission for its proposed march. The order also stated that applications should be disposed of at least a day before the proposed programme or procession after giving the applicant a reasonable opportunity to be heard. It further said that programmes or processions held in violation of the guidelines would be considered unlawful under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS), with the local police authorised to register a suo motu case. In October, the RSS had subsequently approached the Karnataka High Court over the denial of permission for its Chittapur route march. The controversy over the government order has since remained politically contentious. items.title: ‘Travesty of justice’: Over 100 activists, writers seek release of Umar Khalid, Sharjeel Imam
items.summary: More than 100 activists, writers, filmmakers and academics have written an open letter to Chief Justice of India (CJI) Surya Kant seeking the release of student activists Umar Khalid and Sharjeel Imam, who have been in jail without trial for nearly six years under the Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act (UAPA) in relation to the 2020 Delhi riots. The letter, signed by prominent figures including Arundhati Roy, Ramachandra Guha and Amitav Ghosh, expressed concern over the prolonged incarceration of the two activists and said that the UAPA was being used to keep them in custody for an inordinate period without a trial. The signatories referred to a recent lecture delivered by Surya Kant in Sweden, in which he spoke about the Supreme Court's judgment in Union of India v KA Najeeb . In that case, the Supreme Court granted bail to an accused who had spent nearly six years in custody without trial in a UAPA case. The signatories urged the CJI to ensure that the principles laid down in the Najeeb judgment are applied to Umar Khalid and Sharjeel Imam as well. In the Najeeb case, a three-judge bench of the Supreme Court held that even under stringent laws such as the UAPA, an accused cannot be kept in prison indefinitely, particularly when there is little likelihood of the trial being completed within a reasonable period. Surya Kant was a member of the bench that delivered this landmark judgment. The letter pointed out that nearly six years after their arrest, the trial against Umar Khalid and Sharjeel Imam has not begun, despite the prosecution having listed around 900 witnesses. Their bail pleas have also been rejected repeatedly by different courts, including by a two-judge bench of the Supreme Court in January 2026 in the Gulfisha Fatima v State . The January ruling in Gulfisha Fatima v State has subsequently come under scrutiny in another Supreme Court judgment, Syed Iftikhar Andrabi v National Investigation Agency , delivered on May 18, 2026. In that case, Justices BV Nagarathna and Ujjal Bhuyan observed that the earlier two-judge Bench had not only denied bail but had also restricted the accused's ability to seek bail for another year. The Bench further held that the earlier ruling had departed from the principles laid down by the three-judge Bench in KA Najeeb . items.summary: We remember India’s freedom struggle through marches, protests and revolutionaries. But there was another battlefield: the newspaper. Through their newspapers, they challenged the British version of India, exposed colonial excesses, and gave Indians the language of swaraj. items.title: Vande Mataram: The Prevention of Insults to National Honour Bill and legal uncertainties
items.summary: The Union government’s recent moves to formalise the singing and playing of Vande Mataram have brought an old question back into the centre of public debate: how far can the state go in prescribing participation in a national symbol when that symbol also carries contested religious meanings? The question has acquired greater urgency with Union Home Minister Amit Shah introducing the Prevention of Insults to National Honour (Amendment) Bill, 2026, in the Rajya Sabha. The Bill proposes to insert the words “or the national song” into Section 3 of the Prevention of Insults to National Honour Act, 1971. The amendment would extend the existing criminal provision to the national song, making it punishable with imprisonment of up to three years to “intentionally prevent” the singing of the national anthem or national song, or to “cause disturbance” to an assembly engaged in such singing. But the proposed law leaves important questions unanswered. The expressions “intentionally prevents”, “causes disturbance” and “assembly engaged in such singing” are not defined in the legislation. The amendment therefore expands the reach of criminal law to another national symbol without clarifying the precise conduct that could attract punishment. That is particularly significant because the Supreme Court has previously drawn a clear distinction between respectful non-participation and deliberate obstruction of the national anthem. At the same time, a July 9, 2026 order from the Ministry of Home Affairs has asked states, Union Territories and Union government departments to ensure strict compliance with existing orders governing the singing and playing of the national song and national anthem. Taken together, these developments raise questions about whether a framework originally designed to prevent deliberate disruption is now being expanded into a more prescriptive regime around national symbols without adequate safeguards for freedom of conscience. items.title: ECI has no record of what constitutes ‘logical discrepancy’ in SIR, RTI reply shows
items.summary: The Election Commission of India (ECI) has said it has no information on what constitutes a “logical discrepancy” — the category under which many voters were flagged during the second phase of the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls. My Vote, My Right—a coalition of civil society groups—said a member of the coalition filed an RTI application seeking the definition of “logical discrepancies” in any official document, as well as the number of notices issued to voters across the 10 States and Union Territories where the SIR has been completed. In its response, the ECI said the information was not available with the Commission. “The information sought by you is not available in the Commission. It may be available with the Office of the CEO of States/UTs,” the ECI said in its response on August 13. During Phase II of the SIR, the ECI introduced a process to flag voters as having discrepancies, issue them notices, and ask them to produce one of 11 prescribed documents to establish their eligibility to vote. Several voters were informed that “anomalies have been detected” or that “logical discrepancies have been detected” in their records. Media reports have since raised questions about the software and criteria used to flag voters. Reports suggested that voters were flagged for discrepancies such as differences in the spelling of names or where the age gap between a voter and their parent was less than 15 years. In Karnataka, The Hindu reported that the state may have used 10 criteria to identify such discrepancies. However, the ECI has not publicly issued any circular or order defining the criteria under which voters are being flagged. The Chief Electoral Officer of Karnataka has also not provided a written clarification despite civil society organisations repeatedly seeking information about the process, the coalition said. The coalition said the ECI’s RTI response raises questions about the basis on which voters were identified under the “logical discrepancies” category and subjected to additional documentation requirements. It also questioned how such a process was implemented when the ECI itself says it does not have information on the definition of the category or the number of notices issued. My Vote, My Right said the lack of clarity over the criteria and documentation for flagging voters threatens transparency in the electoral roll revision process and could place an additional burden on voters seeking to establish their eligibility. items.title: 16-year-old Class 12 student beaten to death by schoolmates in Chennai
items.summary: Follow TNM’s WhatsApp channel for news updates and story links. A 16-year-old Class 12 student was allegedly beaten to death by a group of students near the Tiruvottiyur bus terminus in Chennai on Friday, August 14. The deceased, identified as Dhanush, was a resident of Vasantha Nagar in Tiruvottiyur and studied at Jai Gopal Garodia Government Higher Secondary School in the area. According to reports, Dhanush’s close friend Jaikesh, also a Class 12 student, had a dispute with Dhanushkumar, a Class 11 student, two days before the incident. The dispute was reportedly over a seniority issue, with Dhanush supporting Jaikesh. Teachers intervened on Thursday and called the students involved, following which the matter was reportedly resolved. Jaikesh was absent from school on Friday. After school hours, around 4.15 pm, Dhanush was waiting for a bus when Dhanushkumar and a group of students allegedly took him to a vacant area behind the school, near the Tiruvottiyur bus terminus. Dhanush was allegedly assaulted by more than 10 students. He reportedly collapsed during the assault and suffered seizures. The group then fled the spot. People who heard the commotion found Dhanush lying unconscious and alerted the police. His school teachers also reached the spot and helped take him to Government Stanley Hospital, where doctors declared him dead on arrival. The police have sent Dhanush’s body for a postmortem examination. The Tiruvottiyur police have registered a murder case and are questioning students, teachers and witnesses to establish the circumstances surrounding the assault and determine the motive. Further investigation is underway.

items.title: NALSAR alumni condemn BCI action against students, call it ‘arbitrary’ and ‘coercive’
items.summary: Follow TNM's WhatsApp channel for news updates and story links. A group of 441 alumni of Hyderabad’s National Academy of Legal Studies and Research (NALSAR) University of Law has condemned the Bar Council of India’s (BCI) intervention in the controversy over students’ opposition to inviting Chief Justice of India Surya Kant to the university’s 2026 convocation, terming the council’s actions “unconstitutional, arbitrary and inhumane”. In a letter to BCI chairman and Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) Rajya Sabha member Manan Kumar Mishra, the alumni said the council had no jurisdiction to enquire into students and faculty for expressing their views on an internal university matter. They also objected to the BCI’s initial decision to prevent the entire 2026 graduating batch from enrolling as advocates. On August 13, the BCI directed State Bar Councils not to enrol NALSAR’s 2026 graduates as advocates and sought a report from Vice-Chancellor Srikrishna Deva Rao identifying students and faculty allegedly involved in organising the campaign against the CJI’s invitation. The enrolment bar was withdrawn within hours following widespread criticism, although the BCI initially said an enquiry would continue. Later, a third clarification was issued, with the BCI chairman saying that even the enquiry would not take place. The alumni said the language used in the BCI’s first communication was particularly troubling, alleging that it sought to identify students and faculty who had drafted, circulated or publicised the representation, organised meetings or communicated with the media. Such activities, they argued, fell within the ambit of free speech. The letter criticised the BCI for using terms such as “groupism”, “dirty politics”, “nasty politics” and “instigating and misguiding students”, saying such language was unbecoming of a statutory body entrusted with regulating legal education and the legal profession. “The BCI has no role in regulating matters of free speech on university campuses,” the alumni said, arguing that its statutory role in legal education was confined to promoting legal education and laying down standards. They said the students had merely communicated their views to the NALSAR Vice-Chancellor and that the matter was internal to the university. “It was no occasion for a statutory body entrusted with regulating the profession and the standards of legal education to call for a witch hunt of students and faculty,” the alumni said.
